summary: Compares win_shell (runs in PowerShell or cmd, supports shell operators and multi-line commands) with win_command (runs a process outside a shell). CMD-only commands like mkdir, del and copy need a cmd.exe /c prefix with win_command.
questions: Should I use win_shell or win_command?
How do I use pipes or redirection in a Windows task?
How do I run a cmd command instead of PowerShell with win_shell?
Why does mkdir fail with win_command?
How do I run multiple PowerShell lines in one task?

answer_card.title: win_shell vs win_command
answer_card.answer_md:
- **`win_shell`** runs in a shell (PowerShell by default, or `cmd.exe` via `args: executable: cmd.exe`) so operators like `<`, `>`, `|`, `;`, `&&`, `||` and multi-line scripts work.
- **`win_command`** runs a process outside a shell. To use shell built-ins, call the shell yourself.

```yaml
- win_shell: Get-Service -Name service | Stop-Service
- win_command: whoami.exe
- win_command: cmd.exe /c mkdir C:\temp
```

CMD-only commands like `mkdir`, `del`, and `copy` must be prefixed with `cmd.exe /c` under `win_command`.
